title: SSC CGL Preparation Strategy 2026: Section-wise Plan, Mocks and Attempt Strategy
description: SSC CGL 2026 preparation strategy: how Tier 1 and Tier 2 fit together, section-wise approach, mock cadence, revision loops and an attempt plan for Tier 1.
intro: SSC CGL is a **speed-and-accuracy exam on a fixed syllabus**, so the way you study matters more than how many hours you log. This guide gives the overall method: what the two tiers actually reward, how to split time across Quant, Reasoning, English and GA, how often to take mocks, and how to attempt a paper. For a day-by-day schedule, pick one of the study plans linked at the end.

sections.title: Plan around both tiers, not just Tier 1
sections.body:
Tier 1 only shortlists you. The merit list comes from **Tier 2 Paper 1, which is out of 390 marks**. Prepare for Tier 1 in a way that does not have to be thrown away for Tier 2.

| | Tier 1 | Tier 2 Paper 1 |
|---|---|---|
| Role | Screening (marks do not carry into merit) | Merit-deciding |
| Questions | 100 (25 per subject) | 130 merit questions + 20 Computer (qualifying) |
| Marks | 200 | 390 (+ 60 Computer, qualifying) |
| Marking | +2 correct, -0.50 wrong | +3 correct, -1 wrong |
| Heaviest module | Equal weight, 50 marks each | English, 45 questions, 135 marks |

Practical meaning:

- Do not stop at "just enough for Tier 1". Topics like Geometry, Trigonometry, Algebra and Cloze Test are Tier 1 questions too, and they are exactly what Tier 2 pushes harder.
- Past cycles have left a gap of a few months between Tier 1 and Tier 2 (see the timeline on the [exam pattern](/exams/ssc-cgl/exam-pattern/) page). Keep your notes and mistake log in a form you can reuse.
- Computer Knowledge and the data-entry speed test (DEST) are qualifying only, so give them small, scheduled slots rather than long ones.

sections.title: Split your study time by marks and weak areas
sections.body:
Use the shift-analysis counts on the [weightage](/exams/ssc-cgl/weightage/) page to decide where an hour earns the most. As a starting split for a full-time aspirant (about 6 hours a day):

| Subject | Share of study time | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Quantitative Aptitude | 35% | Calculation speed is the biggest differentiator; also the section where most people lose time |
| English | 25% | Vocabulary, grammar and comprehension are learnable and carry 45 Tier 2 questions |
| Reasoning | 20% | Quickly improves with pattern practice; cheapest marks if your base is decent |
| General Awareness | 20% | Mostly memory work; fits well into short revision slots |

Adjust it using your mock data. If Reasoning is already 22 or 23 out of 25 at accuracy, move that hour to your weakest section. Working professionals can keep the same ratio at 3 to 4 hours a day and simply plan for a longer runway (see the 60-day and 90-day plans).

sections.title: Section-wise approach: what to study first
sections.body:
**Quantitative Aptitude.** Start with the arithmetic backbone, then move to the advanced blocks.

1. Speed base first: tables to 20, squares to 40, cubes to 20, fraction to percentage equivalents. This is a scored skill since calculators are not allowed.
2. Arithmetic: [Percentage](/quant/percentage/), [Profit, Loss and Discount](/quant/profit-loss-discount/), [Ratio and Proportion](/quant/ratio-proportion/), [Average](/quant/average/), [Time and Work](/quant/time-work/), [Time, Speed and Distance](/quant/time-speed-distance/), [Interest](/quant/interest/).
3. Advanced blocks, which the shift analysis shows are the biggest by question count: [Geometry](/quant/geometry/) and [Data Interpretation](/quant/data-interpretation/), then [Algebra](/quant/algebra/), [Trigonometry](/quant/trigonometry/) and mensuration.

**Reasoning.** Begin with the high-frequency verbal types ([Series](/reasoning/series/), [Analogy](/reasoning/analogy/), [Classification](/reasoning/classification/), [Coding-Decoding](/reasoning/coding-decoding/)), then puzzles ([Seating Arrangement](/reasoning/seating-arrangement/), [Syllogism](/reasoning/syllogism/)), then the figure-based types, which are quick once you know the technique.

**English.** Alternate grammar and vocabulary. [Reading Comprehension](/english/reading-comprehension/) and [Cloze Test](/english/cloze-test/) together make up a large share of the section, so read daily and practise them from the first month. Use the [vocab](/vocab/) page for a daily word habit.

**General Awareness.** Split into three buckets: current affairs (steady daily/weekly input, see [current affairs](/current-affairs/)), static GK and history/polity/geography/economy (revise in cycles), and science (Biology, Physics, Chemistry, mostly class 6 to 10 level). Current affairs and Biology lead the shift counts.

sections.title: The four-step loop for every topic
sections.body:
Use the same loop for each topic so that study turns into marks:

1. **Learn** the concept and the standard method (30 to 45 minutes).
2. **Drill** 20 to 30 questions on that topic, untimed, with the shortcut method after each solution.
3. **Time it**: a 10 to 15 question topic test with a clock.
4. **Log**: write every wrong or slow question in a mistakes notebook with the reason (concept gap, calculation slip, misread, time).

Do not move on from a topic until the timed test is at 80 to 85% accuracy. The mistakes notebook becomes your revision material; re-do its questions every weekend. Keep formulas on one sheet and re-read it twice a week; the [formula sheet](/formula-sheet/) is built for that.

sections.title: Mock cadence and revision loops
sections.body:
Mocks should be introduced earlier than most people expect, and analysed longer than they are attempted.

| Phase | Mocks | Analysis time |
|---|---|---|
| Learning phase | One sectional test per week | 1 hour |
| Build phase | One full mock every 3 to 4 days | 1.5 to 2 hours |
| Final 3 to 4 weeks | One full mock every alternate day | 2 hours, plus re-solving every wrong question |

Rules that keep mocks useful:

- Attempt at the same hour as your exam shift; use the same 60-minute, four-section format. Take the full-length tests on our [mocks](/exams/ssc-cgl/mocks/) page.
- Analyse three things per mock: wrong answers (why), correct but slow answers (what shortcut did you miss) and questions you skipped (were they actually easy).
- Revise in loops: **day 1, day 7, day 21** for each topic. Notes, formula sheet and mistakes notebook, nothing new in the last week.
- Do not compare raw marks across shifts or with friends; SSC normalises scores, so treat your mock score as a trend line, not a verdict. The [score calculator](/exams/ssc-cgl/score-calculator/) helps you estimate your standing.

sections.title: Tier 1 attempt strategy
sections.body:
For the 2026 cycle, the notice reported for Tier 1 gives each subject its own **15-minute timer** inside the 60-minute paper, and unused time in one subject cannot be moved to another. That makes 25 questions in 15 minutes, or roughly 36 seconds per question. Treat this as your working rule and confirm on the notice and your admit card.

- **Two passes inside every section.** First pass: solve what you can in under 30 seconds, mark the rest. Second pass: return to marked questions in the remaining time.
- **Do not leave time on the table.** If General Awareness finishes in 8 minutes, spend the rest re-checking the questions you were unsure of; the clock will not carry it forward.
- **Quant is the time sink.** Skip lengthy calculation questions on the first pass; Data Interpretation sets and Geometry are worth taking only after the quick ones.
- **Negative marking is mild in Tier 1** (-0.50 against +2). A question where you have eliminated two options is usually worth attempting.
- **Target.** Shift analyses on this site put good attempts at roughly 72 to 82 questions with around 85% accuracy for 2025. The 2025 Tier 1 UR cutoff for the main list was 136.83 (see [cutoffs](/exams/ssc-cgl/cutoffs/)); cutoffs move every year, so treat it as a band, not a promise.

sections.title: Mistakes that cost the most
sections.body:
- Buying many books and finishing none. One source per subject plus PYQs is enough.
- Reading solutions instead of solving. If you cannot solve it on a blank page, you have not learnt it.
- Skipping English and GA because "Quant decides". All four sections carry equal weight in Tier 1.
- Taking mocks without analysing them.
- Ignoring the data-entry speed test until the Tier 2 call letter arrives. Practise on a real keyboard using the [typing test](/exams/ssc-cgl/typing-test/).
- Treating a good Tier 1 as the end. It only earns you a seat in Tier 2.

No plan guarantees selection. What a good plan does is make your preparation measurable, so you know what to fix each week.

faqs.q: How many hours a day do I need for SSC CGL?
faqs.a: Full-time aspirants usually work 6 to 8 focused hours. Working candidates can do 3 to 4 hours with a longer runway of 4 to 6 months. Quality (timed practice and mistake review) matters more than total hours.

faqs.q: Should I prepare for Tier 1 and Tier 2 separately?
faqs.a: No. Prepare the syllabus once, at Tier 2 depth where possible, and use mocks to tune speed for Tier 1. Tier 1 marks do not count in final merit, which is built from Tier 2 Paper 1 (out of 390).

faqs.q: Which section should I start with?
faqs.a: Start with Quant arithmetic and basic grammar and vocabulary, since both need the longest build-up. Add Reasoning and General Awareness in parallel in short daily slots.

faqs.q: When should I start taking full mocks?
faqs.a: Start sectional tests in the first month and full mocks once you have covered roughly half the syllabus. In the last 3 to 4 weeks, take a full mock every alternate day and spend as long on analysis as on the attempt.

No. The syllabus is fixed and widely documented. A disciplined schedule, good practice material, regular mocks and honest error analysis are enough for most candidates; coaching helps only if you need accountability.

faqs.q: How do I avoid negative marking?
faqs.a: Attempt only when you can eliminate at least two options, mark doubtful questions for the second pass, and avoid last-minute blind guessing in sections where your accuracy is below 70%.
